section_summary: This section covers U.S. diplomatic reporting from June 1935 to April 1936 concerning Japanese cabinet politics, administrative reorganization, and the February 26 Incident (1936 military coup d'état). It details the creation and deliberations of the Cabinet Deliberative Body and Cabinet Investigation Bureau under the Okada Cabinet, the assassination of prominent statesmen during the February 26 uprising, and the dramatic survival of Prime Minister Okada. It further documents the resignation of the Okada ministry, the political maneuvers and military pressures surrounding the formation of the new cabinet under Prime Minister Koki Hirota, and the appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister.

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the organization, personnel, and political significance of the newly established Cabinet Deliberative Body and Cabinet Investigation Bureau.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes the formation, composition, and functions of the Cabinet Deliberative Body and the Cabinet Investigation Bureau created by imperial ordinances in May 1935. The Deliberative Body functions as a political advisory board composed of peers, business representatives, and politicians, while the Investigation Bureau serves as an expert research commission staffed primarily from the civil bureaucracy with junior military officers. Grew observes that these extra-constitutional bodies reflect public disillusionment with political party rule and a growing demand for centralized national planning, though the military remains wary of subordinating itself to political bodies.
subfiles.title: Despatch Regarding the Cabinet Deliberative Body and the Cabinet Investigation Bureau

subfiles.about: Political report section covering cabinet members' speeches at the Prefectural Governors' Conference and the establishment of new cabinet advisory organs.
subfiles.summary: This section of the Embassy's political report details addresses delivered on May 3, 1935, by Premier Okada, Foreign Minister Hirota, Finance Minister Takahashi, and the Minister of Justice to prefectural governors. Premier Okada implicitly criticized the Minobe organ theory of the Emperor, while Hirota reviewed foreign relations with Manchukuo, the Soviet Union, and China. It also records the May 10 imperial ordinances formally establishing the Cabinet Deliberative Body and Investigation Bureau, detailing the appointments of Finance Minister Takahashi, Viscount Saito, and party representatives, while noting the military's lack of representation in the Deliberative Body.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1348 (Political Report No. 90): Speeches at the Governors' Conference and Creation of Cabinet Organs

subfiles.about: Political report section reviewing the initial meetings and policy deliberations of the Cabinet Deliberative Body and Investigation Bureau.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that the Cabinet Deliberative Body and the Cabinet Investigation Bureau held their first meeting on June 12, 1935, taking up the reform of central and local finances. At a second session on June 17, members discussed policies for emergency finances and national economic promotion, interpellating cabinet ministers. The War and Navy Ministers declined to give specific views on adjusting defense expenditures to national finance, citing the need for prior study of comparative foreign army strengths, conditions in Manchukuo, and the outcome of the upcoming naval limitation conference.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1387 (Political Report No. 91): Meetings of the Cabinet Deliberative Body and Investigation Bureau

subfiles.about: Telegram and memorandum reporting the resignation of War Minister Hayashi and the appointment of General Yoshiyuki Kawashima.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville reports the resignation of the Minister of War and the immediate appointment of General Yoshiyuki Kawashima, former commander of forces in Korea, without apparent political complications. An accompanying State Department memorandum characterizes Kawashima as an able administrator and strong leader unaligned with either the Araki or Ugaki factions. Consequently, he is expected to carry forward General Hayashi's efforts to suppress factionalism within the Imperial Japanese Army.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 171 and Memorandum Regarding Appointment of General Yoshiyuki Kawashima as Minister of War

subfiles.about: Telegram conveying report received from Foreign Minister Hirota via the Japanese Ambassador in Moscow regarding the February 26 coup d'état.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Bullitt transmits news received from Japanese Ambassador Ota in Moscow based on an urgent telegram from Foreign Minister Hirota. First Division officers in Tokyo mutinied in the early hours of February 26, 1936, murdering Prime Minister Okada, Finance Minister Takahashi, and Viscount Saito, while Count Makino narrowly escaped assassination. A state of danger of war was proclaimed and financial exchanges were temporarily closed, though calm reportedly returned to the capital and no foreign office officials were attacked. Ambassador Ota noted the extreme difficulty of selecting a new premier, speculating that General Araki or General Ugaki might be chosen.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 67 from Moscow Concerning the February 26 Coup d'État

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Home Minister Goto's appointment as temporary Acting Premier and confirming Count Makino's safety.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports an extra edition of the Tokyo Nichi Nichi announcing that Home Minister Goto has been named temporary Acting Premier following the reported assassination of Premier Okada. The Embassy also learned from a reliable informant who spoke directly with Count Makino that Makino was neither killed nor wounded during the uprising.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 39 Concerning Appointment of Home Minister Goto as Acting Premier and Count Makino's Safety

subfiles.about: Extensive telegram detailing the February 26 military insurrection, assassinations of senior officials, and the political motivations of the rebels.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive four-part report on the military coup d'état launched in Tokyo by extremist young army officers seeking a Showa Restoration. Rebel units established cordons around government offices and the Imperial Palace, keeping the Emperor incommunicado while assassinating Viscount Saito, Inspector General Watanabe, and reportedly Premier Okada and Finance Minister Takahashi, and wounding Grand Chamberlain Suzuki. A manifesto signed by Captains Nonaka and Ando accused the government of usurping imperial prerogatives and cited the London Naval Treaty and General Mazaki's dismissal. The rebellion appears to have been precipitated by recent liberal election victories and the court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 37 Concerning the February 26 Military Uprising and Coup d'État in Tokyo

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Soviet information on the suppression of the Tokyo mutiny and prospects for the premiership.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Bullitt transmits intelligence provided by Soviet Foreign Commissar Litvinov from the Soviet Ambassador in Tokyo. Prince Saionji advised the Emperor to refuse negotiations with the mutineers and crush the uprising with utmost severity, while loyal government troops established firm control over the capital. Litvinov stated that General Mazaki had no prospect of becoming Prime Minister, with Prince Konoe, President of the House of Peers, expected to receive the mandate, which Moscow regarded as an encouraging sign against extreme militarist rule. Chinese Ambassador Yen also indicated that increased Japanese pressure on China was unlikely for several weeks.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 73 from Moscow Concerning Suppression of the Mutiny and Prospective Premiership

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that Prime Minister Okada survived the assassination attempt uninjured and resumed the premiership.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports information received from Baron Hayashi confirming that Prime Minister Okada is alive and uninjured, having escaped assassination when his brother-in-law was mistaken for him and killed. Okada remained in hiding since the night of February 25 before presenting himself to the Emperor, whereupon Acting Prime Minister Goto resigned and Okada resumed the premiership to the Emperor's great satisfaction. Grew observes that these dramatic developments may cause a nationwide public reaction against the military and yield salutary political results.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 51 Concerning Prime Minister Okada's Survival and Reappearance

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the restoration of normal conditions in Tokyo, Captain Nonaka's suicide, and the dismissal of rebel officers.
keywords: Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that virtually normal conditions have returned to Tokyo, with street barricades removed, civilian police resuming patrols, and emergency troops withdrawing. An official announcement stated that only Captain Nonaka committed suicide, while the remaining rebel officers are imprisoned and have been summarily dismissed in disgrace from the army without trial. No announcement has yet been made regarding the formation of a new cabinet or the appointment of a new Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 52 Concerning Restoration of Normal Conditions and Arrest of Rebel Officers

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Prince Saionji's consultations in Tokyo and the Okada Cabinet's functioning as a provisional government.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Prince Saionji arrived in Tokyo on March 2 and initiated consultations with various national leaders before formulating his recommendations to the Throne regarding the next cabinet. Japanese newspapers editorially demand a strong national cabinet capable of stabilizing the country, though conditions remain too unsettled to predict ministerial personnel. Meanwhile, the Okada Cabinet, having resigned en bloc on February 26 to assume responsibility for the insurrection, continues to carry out its duties as a provisional government.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 56 Concerning Consultations by Prince Saionji and the Provisional Okada Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting unconfirmed accounts that Prince Fumimaro Konoe has been instructed to form a cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that news agencies have published reports that Prince Konoe has been instructed to endeavor to form a Cabinet. The Embassy has been unable to obtain official confirmation, but Japanese officials interviewed indicated a willingness to accept the reports as trustworthy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 58 Concerning Reports of Prince Konoe Receiving the Imperial Command

subfiles.about: Telegram announcing that Foreign Minister Koki Hirota has received the Imperial command to form a cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the official announcement that Foreign Minister Koki Hirota has received the Imperial command to form a Cabinet. Hirota has immediately entered into conferences with various political and military leaders to compose the new administration.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 60 Concerning Foreign Minister Hirota's Imperial Command to Form a Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting army difficulties obstructing Hirota's cabinet formation, alongside appointments of Yuasa and Matsudaira to imperial court posts.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Hirota's efforts to form a Cabinet have encountered obstacles, apparently from the army, and he has not yet succeeded. Concurrently, Kurahei Yuasa has been appointed Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal, and Tsuneo Matsudaira, former Ambassador to Great Britain, has been appointed Imperial Household Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 61 Concerning Hirota's Cabinet Difficulties with the Army and Court Appointments

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting a General Staff officer's briefing on the coup and General Terauchi's statement of army conditions for the new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits confidential explanations given by a General Staff officer to Military Attaché Lieutenant Colonel Crane. The officer explained that the February 26 incident was carried out by an ignorant radical fringe of officers who misled their men into believing they were participating in night maneuvers. Senior generals on the Supreme Military Council, including Araki, Mazaki, and Minami, are retiring to assume responsibility, making General Terauchi the senior candidate for War Minister. The army approves of Hirota but demands a vigorous, progressive cabinet dedicated to radical administrative renovation and strong national defense, rejecting any compromise with liberalism or the status quo.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 63 Concerning General Staff Explanations of the Coup and the Army's Cabinet Demands

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Hirota's successful organization of a cabinet, detailing key ministerial appointments and political alignments.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Hirota has succeeded in forming a Cabinet, temporarily retaining the Foreign Affairs portfolio due to army opposition to Shigeru Yoshida. Important appointments include Eiichi Baba as Finance Minister, Count Terauchi as War Minister, Osami Nagano as Navy Minister, Keinosuke Ushio as Home and Education Minister, and Raisaburo Hayashi as Justice Minister. Baba is a respected conservative banker, Terauchi is an independent senior officer with no factional ties, and Ushio and Hayashi represent experienced legal and administrative leadership. The cabinet has secured the support of the two major political parties and satisfies army demands for administrative reform.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 65 Concerning the Formation and Personnel of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: State Department biographical memorandum assessing Koki Hirota upon his appointment as Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum reviews the diplomatic background and political standing of Koki Hirota. Born in Fukuoka, Hirota graduated from Tokyo Imperial University in 1905 and served in diplomatic posts in Peking, London, Washington, The Hague, and Moscow prior to his 1933 appointment as Foreign Minister. The memorandum emphasizes Hirota's unique relationship with the patriotic Black Dragon Society (Kokuryukai) and nationalist leaders Mitsuru Toyama and Ryohei Uchida, which has enabled him to maintain military confidence without aligning with political parties.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Koki Hirota

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck examining Hirota's premiership and its potential effect on China policy.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records a memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, dated March 5, 1936, filed under 894.00/614. The memorandum evaluates the political crisis in Tokyo following the February 26 incident and assesses the likely effects of Koki Hirota's appointment as Prime Minister on Japan's policy toward China.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Hornbeck Memorandum on Hirota as Premier and China Policy

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting an interview with Prime Minister Hirota outlining foreign policies toward the Soviet Union, China, and the United States.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on a comprehensive interview with Prime Minister Hirota, who confirmed that his former foreign policy will continue unchanged under his premiership with full cabinet concurrence. Regarding Soviet Russia, Hirota noted army desires for defense parity in Manchuria, but affirmed there would be no war while he was in office. On China, Hirota explained his three-point policy—stopping anti-Japanese activity, regularizing relations with Manchukuo, and joint opposition to communism—while assuring Grew that the Open Door would be respected. Grew informally raised American domestic concerns regarding surging imports of cheap Japanese manufactured textiles.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 Concerning an Interview with Prime Minister Hirota on Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential telegram reporting Prime Minister Hirota's tentative intention to appoint Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports information obtained from high official authority that Prime Minister Hirota tentatively plans to offer the Ministry for Foreign Affairs to Hachiro Arita upon the latter's return from China. The Embassy was requested to treat this pending appointment as strictly confidential.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 76 Concerning the Intended Appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Telegram from Nanking reporting Japanese Embassy denials of press claims that Ambassador Arita would not return to China.
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy Peck reports from Nanking that a Japanese Embassy official denied reports published by the semi-official Central News Agency stating that Ambassador Arita would not return to China. Japanese diplomat Ando informed Peck that Arita's future assignment had not yet been formally decided.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 57 from Nanking Concerning Japanese Reports on Arita's Future

subfiles.about: Political report section quoting Prime Minister Okada's annual New Year statement on national prestige, Manchukuo, and elections.
subfiles.summary: This section of the Embassy's political report quotes Prime Minister Okada's annual New Year statement. Okada expressed satisfaction over the enhancement of Japan's national prestige and the sound growth of Manchukuo, reaffirmed Japanese claims at the London Naval Conference, pledged honest administration of upcoming Diet elections, and advocated that parliamentary government be allowed to bear fruit.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1693 (Political Report No. 98): Annual New Year Statement by Premier Okada

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a State Department memorandum by Cabot Coville on the military coup and new cabinet composition.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records a memorandum by Cabot Coville of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, dated March 17, 1936, filed under 894.00/629. The memorandum analyzes the Tokyo military coup d'état of February 26 and details the formation and ministerial composition of the new cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Coville Memorandum on the Coup and New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 75 transmitting the Hirota Cabinet's official policy statement and public reactions.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Telegram No. 75 from Ambassador Grew, dated March 18, 1936, filed under 894.00/616. The telegram transmits and comments on the official declaration of policy issued by the Hirota Cabinet and reports on domestic national reaction thereto.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Telegram No. 75 on the Hirota Cabinet Policy Statement

subfiles.about: Telegram and Department paraphrase reporting the formal assumption of office by Hachiro Arita as Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Hachiro Arita, recently Japanese Ambassador to China, has been appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs and formally assumed office on the evening of April 2, 1936. An official Department of State paraphrase of the telegram is attached.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 84 and Paraphrase Regarding Installation of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: State Department biographical memorandum evaluating Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita and assessing prospects for Japan's China policy.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum examines the career and policy views of Hachiro Arita upon his installation as Foreign Minister in the Hirota Cabinet. It reviews his prior assignments in Washington, Peiping, Berlin, Vienna, Brussels, and China, emphasizing his leadership of the moderate Foreign Office group during the 1932-1933 dispute with chauvinist spokesman Toshio Shiratori over the League of Nations. While noting Arita's friendly reputation toward the United States, the memorandum observes that the military approved his appointment after rejecting Shigeru Yoshida, suggesting that no substantial change in Japanese policy toward China should be anticipated.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Hachiro Arita

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a memorandum by Under Secretary Phillips on a conversation with the Japanese Ambassador regarding Arita's appointment.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes a memorandum by Under Secretary of State William Phillips, dated March 17, 1936, filed under 894.00/626. The memorandum details discussions with Japanese Ambassador Hirosi Saito regarding the political situation in Tokyo, reporting that Ambassador to China Arita would be appointed Foreign Minister and that domestic political agitation would likely subside.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Phillips Memorandum on Arita's Appointment as Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 1736 from Tokyo reporting on the formation of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 1736 from Ambassador Grew, dated March 18, 1936, filed under 894.00/637. The despatch provides a comprehensive account of the negotiations and political circumstances leading to the formation of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Despatch No. 1736 on the Formation of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 1733 analyzing the policies of the Hirota Cabinet and domestic public reactions.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 1733 from Ambassador Grew, dated March 19, 1936, filed under 894.00/638. The despatch analyzes the official policies of the newly installed Hirota Cabinet and evaluates public and editorial opinion across Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Despatch No. 1733 on the Policy of the Hirota Cabinet and Public Opinion

subfiles.about: Consular despatch enclosing a local editorial translation and reporting civilian and military reactions in Harbin to the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Consul LaMont transmits a report and translated editorial from the Harbin Nichinichi assessing reactions in Manchuria to the Hirota Cabinet, accompanied by a State Department summary memorandum. The military-aligned newspaper welcomed Hirota's pledges of a strong foreign policy while criticizing his past conciliation, asserting that the Tokyo incident solidified military control over national policy. Local Japanese civilians expressed relief at the resolution of the cabinet crisis, but voiced anxiety that military dominance and new financial policies might provoke a disastrous war with the Soviet Union, though immediate conflict was not considered probable.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 335 from Harbin Concerning Local Reactions to the Formation of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 1758 from Tokyo reporting on subsequent policy developments of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 1758 from Ambassador Grew, dated April 11, 1936, filed under 894.00/643. The despatch details ongoing political and administrative policy developments under the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Despatch No. 1758 on Policy Developments of the Hirota Cabinet
